answer.label: Not George Bernard Shaw — earliest match is critic James Agate
answer.authorDates: 1877–1947 · English theatre critic of The Sunday Times
answer.sourceLine: The line is not Shaw’s. The earliest close match found by Quote Investigator ↗ is a theatre review by James Agate in The Sunday Times of London, April 1926 — and Agate was jeering at Russia, not America. The barb was turned on the United States by an unsigned 1932 editorial in the Paris paper La Liberté, then drifted onto one famous wit after another. Shaw’s name was attached only in 1967; Shaw had died in 1950. QI credits Agate “tentatively” and finds no substantive evidence of coinage for any of the celebrities.

source.heading: The earliest documented wording

docMeta.dd: The Sunday Times (London), 4 April 1926, p. 4 — a review of Andreyev’s Katerina; reprinted in Red Letter Nights (Jonathan Cape, 1944), p. 113

source.excerpt: … the temptation is to cast about for excuses, to pity Russia for having been left out of the Roman march, and so passing from barbarism to decadence without knowing civilization …
trail: April 1926 — the earliest close match. James Agate’s Sunday Times notice of Andreyev’s Katerina pities Russia for “passing from barbarism to decadence without knowing civilisation” — Quote Investigator’s transcription of the newspaper printing. The review is reprinted on p. 113 of Red Letter Nights (1944) ↗, which sets the word “civilization.”

July 1932 — the target becomes America. Furious with President Hoover over war debts, the Paris paper La Liberté wrote that “Americans are the only race which passed directly from barbarism to decadence without knowing civilization” — translated in Time, 25 July 1932 ↗. The author was unnamed.

December 1945 — the best-known celebrity credit. Hans Bendix credited the line to Georges Clemenceau in The Saturday Review of Literature, the earliest such reference recorded by Wikiquote ↗. Churchill, Mencken and Wilde followed — though a variant had already been assigned to the novelist John O’Hara in 1934.

1967 — Shaw’s turn. A Boston Globe interview with H. Rap Brown ascribed the saying to George Bernard Shaw, the ascription Quote Investigator identifies ↗ as the root of the Shaw credit. Shaw had died in 1950.
source.excerptNote: Read directly from the full text of Red Letter Nights, p. 113, and spelled as the book spells it. The review is dated 3 April 1926 in the book; Quote Investigator cites the newspaper printing as The Sunday Times of 4 April 1926, and transcribes the word as “civilisation” where the 1944 Cape reprint sets “civilization.”

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for the famous America wording, because no author or first publication has ever been identified for it — its earliest documented appearance is an unsigned 1932 editorial in La Liberté. The closest documented antecedent, James Agate’s Sunday Times review, was first published in April 1926 and is therefore in the public domain in the United States — but that is a different sentence, about Russia.

author.name: James Agate
author.heading: Who James Agate was
author.metaLine: 1877–1947 · English theatre critic and diarist, The Sunday Times
author.bio: James Agate was the most-read theatre critic in Britain between the wars, writing the weekly drama column of The Sunday Times from 1923 until his death in 1947, and keeping the sprawling published diary Ego. He was a professional phrase-maker — the sort of writer who tossed off a lethal formulation in the middle of a notice and moved on. The barbarism-to-decadence jibe appears exactly that way: buried mid-paragraph in a grumpy 1926 review of a Russian play, aimed at Russia, and never claimed by him as an epigram at all.

misattribution.heading: Five famous names, none of them documented
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most heavily reassigned epigrams in English. Quote Investigator ↗ catalogues the whole parade and concludes that “none of these attributions provides substantive evidence of coinage.”

items.why: QI traces the Shaw ascription to a 1967 Boston Globe interview ↗ with H. Rap Brown, who told the reporter “You know what George Bernard Shaw said about America?” Shaw died in 1950. Wikiquote’s George Bernard Shaw page ↗ carries no entry for the line in any section.

The Times of London ran the exact modern wording as number four in a 2008 “Top Ten Quotes of Oscar Wilde” feature. As QI points out ↗, Wilde died in 1900 — before any evidence of the expression in English.

First recorded by the Danish illustrator Hans Bendix in The Saturday Review of Literature, 1 December 1945, quoting his aunt quoting Clemenceau. Wikiquote ↗ flags this as the earliest such reference; QI has located no direct evidence for Clemenceau.

A Leonard Lyons column in the Washington Post of 29 April 1947 has Churchill using a version while joking about a lecture fee. QI allows ↗ he may well have repeated it — fifteen years after it was already in print.

The Golden Book magazine assigned a variant to the novelist in October 1934, and the Penguin Dictionary of Modern Humorous Quotations repeated it in 1986. QI judges ↗ it unlikely he originated the phrase.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest close match anyone has found is James Agate, writing in The Sunday Times in April 1926 about a Russian play — a sentence you can read for yourself on page 113 of his Red Letter Nights ↗. The famous America version has no identified author at all.

context.heading: Why this one keeps changing owners
lead: The saying is a floating epigram: short, quotable, and structurally anonymous. For more than a decade after 1932 it circulated in English with no author at all — attributed only to “a French journalist,” “a foreign wit,” “an overseas critic,” or, in Ogden Nash’s 1934 verse, “one of those witty Frenchmen whose name I cannot for the moment recall.” A line that good does not stay ownerless for long.

What happened next is the standard mechanism behind most famous fake quotes. An unowned epigram gets assigned to whichever celebrated wit the speaker finds most plausible, and the assignment hardens into a citation. Clemenceau, Churchill, Wilde, Mencken, John O’Hara and Shaw have all been named — every one of them years after the remark was already in print unattributed.
context.detailsSummary: The oddity: Agate was writing about Russia
detailsBody: Agate’s 1926 sentence is not about America. Reviewing Leonid Andreyev’s Katerina at a London theatre, he suggested the English temptation was “to pity Russia for having been left out of the Roman march,” and so passing from barbarism to decadence without knowing civilisation. The target swapped to the United States six years later, in a French paper furious with President Hoover over war debts.

Quote Investigator also notes a partial thematic precursor in French — an 1841 passage by Hippolyte Roux-Ferrand about a Russian ruler who “made his country pass without transition from barbarism to decadence” — and a conceptually similar riff by Henry James about American fruit going from crudity to rottenness with no ripeness in between. QI notes it has not searched French-language newspaper databases, so an earlier French antecedent remains possible.
context.pull: For over a decade the line had no author at all — only “one of those witty Frenchmen whose name I cannot for the moment recall.”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator tentatively credits James Agate (1926, about Russia) with coining the phrase, documents the 1932 La Liberté application to America, and traces the Shaw credit to a 1967 Boston Globe interview with H. Rap Brown; it also covers the Wilde (2008 Times), Clemenceau (1945 Bendix), Churchill (1947 Lyons) and O'Hara (1934) attributions and finds none provides substantive evidence of coinage.

The full text of James Agate's Red Letter Nights contains, on p. 113 in the Katerina review, the words 'passing from barbarism to decadence without knowing civilization', applied to Russia; the review is dated April 3, 1926 at its end.
Time magazine of 25 July 1932 quotes the Paris newspaper La Liberté: 'Americans are the only race which passed directly from barbarism to decadence without knowing civilization.'

Wikiquote's Georges Clemenceau page records the America/barbarism/degeneration line as attributed to Clemenceau by Hans Bendix in 'Merry Christmas, America!', The Saturday Review of Literature, 1 December 1945, p. 9 — the earliest such reference — and notes similar remarks are attributed without a source to Oscar Wilde and George Bernard Shaw; it also lists the variant 'America is the only country that went from barbarism to decadence without civilisation in between.'
Wikiquote's George Bernard Shaw page contains no entry for 'barbarism to decadence' in any section, including Misattributed and Disputed.

Henry James's story 'A Bundle of Letters' contains the passage about a nation reaching an ultimate stage of evolution without the mediate one — 'the passage of the fruit, in other words, from crudity to rottenness, without the interposition of a period of useful (and ornamental) ripeness' — applied to Americans.

James Agate (9 September 1877 – 6 June 1947) was an English diarist and theatre critic who was drama critic of The Sunday Times from 1923 to 1947, and Red Letter Nights (Jonathan Cape, 1944) appears in his bibliography.
George Bernard Shaw lived 26 July 1856 – 2 November 1950 and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.
